solarSystem.name: Sun (Sol)
funFacts: Contains 99.86% of the entire mass of our Solar System and fuses ~600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second.
Orbits the Milky Way Galactic Center at ~230 km/s—taking ~225 million years ("one cosmic year") per revolution.
Light from the Sun’s core takes up to 100,000 years to bounce to the surface, then just 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.

solarSystem.name: Mercury
funFacts: Smallest planet in our Solar System—slightly smaller in diameter than Jupiter’s moon Ganymede and Saturn’s moon Titan.
Despite being closest to the Sun, permanently shadowed craters at its poles hold billions of tons of water ice.
A solar day on Mercury (sunrise to sunrise) lasts 176 Earth days—twice as long as its 88-day year!

solarSystem.name: Venus
funFacts: Hottest planet in the Solar System (464°C / 867°F) due to a runaway CO₂ greenhouse atmosphere 92× denser than Earth’s.
Rotates backwards (retrograde) so slowly that a sidereal day on Venus (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 days).
Often called Earth’s twin in size (0.95 Earth radii), with sulfuric acid clouds reflecting 75% of incoming sunlight.

solarSystem.name: Earth (Terra)
funFacts: Default cosmic reference origin (0.00 km). Orbits the Sun at 29.78 km/s while riding the Sun’s 230 km/s orbit through the Milky Way.
Densest planet in the Solar System (5.51 g/cm³) and the only world confirmed to harbor surface liquid oceans and life.
Surrounded by thousands of active spacecraft and satellites in Low, Medium, and Geostationary Earth Orbit.

solarSystem.name: Moon (Luna)
funFacts: Drifting away from Earth by ~3.8 cm per year due to tidal angular momentum transfer—measured via Apollo laser retroreflectors.
Fifth largest moon in the Solar System and the largest moon relative to the size of its host planet.
Formed ~4.5 billion years ago from debris after a Mars-sized protoplanet (Theia) collided with early Earth.

solarSystem.name: Mars
funFacts: Home to Olympus Mons—the tallest volcano in the Solar System at 21.9 km high (nearly 2.5× Mount Everest).
Valles Marineris canyon stretches 4,000 km across Mars—wide enough to span the entire continental United States.
Currently inhabited exclusively by human-built robotic explorers including Curiosity, Perseverance, and orbital reconnaissance craft.

solarSystem.name: Jupiter
funFacts: 2.5× more massive than all other Solar System planets combined, spinning once every 9 hours 55 minutes—fastest of any planet.
The Great Red Spot is a centuries-old anticyclonic storm wider than Earth with 430+ km/h winds.
Hosts 95 confirmed moons, including Europa—whose subsurface salt-water ocean holds roughly twice the water of Earth’s oceans.

solarSystem.name: Saturn
funFacts: Saturn’s main rings span 282,000 km across yet have a typical vertical thickness of just 10 meters!
Mean density is 0.687 g/cm³—less dense than liquid water.
Its moon Enceladus shoots geysers of organic-rich water vapor from a warm subsurface ocean directly into space, while Titan has liquid methane lakes.

solarSystem.name: Uranus
funFacts: Knocked onto its side with a 97.77° axial tilt—rolling around the Sun with 21-year-long polar summers and winters.
JWST’s near-infrared camera recently revealed 11 of Uranus’s 13 dusty rings and glowing polar cloud caps in stunning clarity.
Records the coldest planetary atmospheric temperature in the Solar System at 49 K (-224°C).

solarSystem.name: Neptune
funFacts: Experiences supersonic winds reaching 2,100 km/h—the fastest sustained planetary winds in the Solar System.
Completed its very first full 164.8-year orbit since its 1846 discovery in July 2011.
Deep inside Ice Giants like Neptune and Uranus, extreme pressure may compress carbon into "diamond rain".

solarSystem.name: Pluto
funFacts: New Horizons revealed Tombaugh Regio—a 1,000-km-wide heart-shaped nitrogen-ice glacier actively convecting on Pluto.
Forms a binary-like system with its large moon Charon; their shared center of mass lies in empty space between them.
Orbits in the Kuiper Belt with a tilted 17° inclination and eccentric 248-year orbit.

zodiacSigns.name: Aries
zodiacSigns.title: The Ram
zodiacSigns.funFact: Contains Hamal, an orange giant star 66 light-years away hosting a confirmed gas giant exoplanet 1.8× Jupiter’s mass.

zodiacSigns.name: Taurus
zodiacSigns.title: The Bull
zodiacSigns.funFact: Home to both the Pleiades (Seven Sisters) star cluster and the Crab Nebula (M1), remnant of a supernova seen on Earth in 1054 AD.

zodiacSigns.name: Gemini
zodiacSigns.title: The Twins
zodiacSigns.funFact: Castor is actually a sextuple star system of six gravitationally bound stars, while Pollux hosts the exoplanet Thestias.

zodiacSigns.name: Cancer
zodiacSigns.title: The Crab
zodiacSigns.funFact: Contains the Beehive Cluster (M44) and 55 Cancri, a famous multi-planet system featuring the lava super-Earth 55 Cancri e.

zodiacSigns.name: Leo
zodiacSigns.title: The Lion
zodiacSigns.funFact: Our entire Solar System is hurtling at 369.8 km/s toward the direction of Leo relative to the Cosmic Microwave Background!

zodiacSigns.name: Virgo
zodiacSigns.title: The Maiden
zodiacSigns.funFact: Looks straight toward the Virgo Cluster of ~1,500 galaxies 54 million light-years away, including M87 and its supermassive black hole.

zodiacSigns.name: Libra
zodiacSigns.title: The Scales
zodiacSigns.funFact: Hosts Gliese 581, one of the earliest red dwarf systems discovered with multiple rocky and super-Earth exoplanets.

zodiacSigns.name: Scorpius
zodiacSigns.title: The Scorpion
zodiacSigns.funFact: Antares ("Rival of Mars") is a red supergiant ~680× wider than our Sun—if placed at our Sun, its surface would swallow Mars’s orbit.

zodiacSigns.name: Sagittarius
zodiacSigns.title: The Archer
zodiacSigns.funFact: Points directly at the heart of our Milky Way Galaxy and Sagittarius A*, a 4.15-million-solar-mass supermassive black hole.

zodiacSigns.name: Capricornus
zodiacSigns.title: The Sea-Goat
zodiacSigns.funFact: In 1846, German astronomer Johann Galle discovered the planet Neptune inside Capricornus within 1° of Urbain Le Verrier’s mathematical prediction.

zodiacSigns.name: Aquarius
zodiacSigns.title: The Water-Bearer
zodiacSigns.funFact: Home to both the Helix Nebula ("Eye of God") and TRAPPIST-1, an ultra-cool dwarf star with SEVEN Earth-sized rocky planets!

zodiacSigns.name: Pisces
zodiacSigns.title: The Fishes
zodiacSigns.funFact: Contains the Vernal Equinox point (0° Right Ascension) where the Sun crosses the celestial equator northward every March.

landmarks.name: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)
landmarks.nasaQuery: James Webb Space Telescope mirror artist deployment
funFacts: Stationed in a halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 Lagrange point ~1.5 million km beyond Earth.
6.5-meter gold-coated beryllium primary mirror observes infrared light from the earliest galaxies formed <300 Myr after the Big Bang.
5-layer tennis-court-sized sunshield keeps its instruments cooled below 50 K (-223°C).

landmarks.name: Voyager 1
funFacts: Farthest human-made object in the universe (~167 AU / ~25 billion km from Earth), traveling through interstellar space at 17.0 km/s.
Crossed the heliopause into the interstellar medium in August 2012 and carries the Golden Record of Earth sounds & images.
Even as the fastest escaping probe, it would take ~74,000 years to reach Proxima Centauri’s distance.

landmarks.name: Helix Nebula (NGC 7293)
funFacts: Nicknamed the "Eye of God"—one of the closest bright planetary nebulae to Earth at just 655 light-years in Aquarius.
Created by a dying Sun-like star shedding its outer gas shells while its hot white dwarf core illuminates the expanding 5.7-light-year ring.
Contains over 40,000 "cometary knots" of dust—each wider than our entire Solar System out to Pluto.

landmarks.name: Orion Nebula (M42)
funFacts: Closest massive star-forming region to Earth (1,344 ly), visible to the naked eye as the fuzzy middle "star" in Orion’s sword.
Spanning 24 light-years across, it harbors over 700 newborn stars and protoplanetary disks ("proplyds") actively forming new solar systems.
JWST discovered candidate free-floating planetary-mass binary objects ("JuMBOs") inside the Trapezium cluster.

landmarks.name: Ring Nebula (M57)
funFacts: 3D spectroscopic mapping proves M57 isn’t a flat ring—it is a barrel-shaped football of glowing ionized gas pointed almost directly at Earth!
JWST revealed 20,000 dense hydrogen globules and 10 concentric arcs sculpted by an unseen binary companion star.

landmarks.name: Pillars of Creation (Eagle Nebula M16)
funFacts: Towering columns of cool interstellar hydrogen and dust 4 to 5 light-years tall—tall enough to bridge from our Sun to Alpha Centauri!
Crimson lava-like edges in JWST’s view are supersonic jets launched by infant protostars still cocooned inside the dust fingers.

landmarks.name: Crab Nebula (M1)
landmarks.nasaQuery: Crab Nebula M1 Hubble Chandra Webb
funFacts: Expanding debris cloud from SN 1054—a supernova recorded by Chinese, Japanese, and Indigenous astronomers on July 4, 1054 AD, bright enough to see in daylight!
At its core spins the Crab Pulsar: a city-sized neutron star rotating 30.2 times EVERY SECOND while whipping out relativistic X-ray jets.

landmarks.name: Cygnus X-1
funFacts: First X-ray source widely accepted as a black hole (and the subject of a famous 1974 scientific wager between Stephen Hawking and Kip Thorne).
Weighs 21.2 solar masses compressed inside an event horizon just ~125 km across, siphoning stellar wind from a blue supergiant companion.

landmarks.name: Cosmic Cliffs — Carina Nebula (NGC 3324)
funFacts: Subject of JWST’s iconic First Deep Field release: jagged "mountains" of gas reaching 7 light-years high sculpted by blistering ultraviolet stellar winds.
Contains Eta Carinae, a hypergiant star system shining 5 million times brighter than the Sun.

landmarks.name: Sagittarius A* (Milky Way Galactic Center)
landmarks.nasaQuery: Sagittarius A black hole Galactic Center
funFacts: Gravitational anchor of our Milky Way Galaxy: 4.15 million solar masses packed within Mercury’s orbital radius.
Directly imaged by the planet-sized Event Horizon Telescope array in 2022; star S2 whips past it at 7,650 km/s (2.55% the speed of light!).

landmarks.name: Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC)
funFacts: Largest satellite galaxy orbiting the Milky Way (~30 billion stars) and site of SN 1987A, the closest supernova observed since the invention of the telescope.
Contains the Tarantula Nebula—so luminous that if placed at the Orion Nebula’s distance, it would cast visible shadows on Earth at night!

landmarks.name: Andromeda Galaxy (M31)
funFacts: Nearest major spiral galaxy to the Milky Way at 2.537 million light-years—and the farthest object easily visible to the unaided human eye!
Contains ~1 trillion stars (roughly double the Milky Way) and is approaching us at 110 km/s, set to merge into "Milkomeda" in ~4.5 billion years.

landmarks.name: Triangulum Galaxy (M33)
funFacts: Third-largest member of the Local Group (~40 billion stars), gravitationally linked to neighboring Andromeda.

landmarks.name: Centaurus A (NGC 5128)
funFacts: Closest active galactic nucleus (AGN) to Earth, shooting twin relativistic plasma jets spanning over a million light-years into intergalactic space.

landmarks.name: Whirlpool Galaxy (M51)
funFacts: First galaxy ever classified as having spiral structure (Lord Rosse, 1845), locked in a tidal gravitational dance with companion galaxy NGC 5195.

landmarks.name: Sombrero Galaxy (M104)
funFacts: Viewed 6° north of its equatorial dust ring; hosts ~2,000 globular star clusters (10× more than the Milky Way) and a 1-billion-solar-mass central black hole.

landmarks.name: Messier 87 & M87* Supermassive Black Hole
landmarks.nasaQuery: M87 black hole Event Horizon Hubble jet
funFacts: Humanity’s first ever direct image of a black hole shadow (EHT, 2019), anchoring the center of the Virgo Cluster.
Weighs 6.5 BILLION solar masses—its event horizon (38 billion km across) is more than 3× wider than Pluto’s entire orbit!

landmarks.name: The Great Attractor / Laniakea Core
funFacts: Gravitational focal valley of our home Laniakea Supercluster (~100,000 galaxies spanning 520 million light-years, massing 10¹⁷ Suns).
Hidden behind the Milky Way’s dusty "Zone of Avoidance", pulling the Local Group toward Norma & Shapley at ~600+ km/s.

landmarks.name: Coma Cluster (Abell 1656)
funFacts: Where Fritz Zwicky first inferred the existence of Dark Matter in 1933 after measuring galaxies orbiting far too fast for visible matter alone to hold together.

landmarks.name: Boötes Void ("The Great Nothing")
funFacts: An immense 330-million-light-year-wide spherical cavern in the Cosmic Web containing only ~60 galaxies where ~2,000 would normally exist.
Astronomer Greg Aldering remarked: "If the Milky Way had been in the center of the Boötes Void, we wouldn’t have known there were other galaxies until the 1960s."

landmarks.name: Sloan Great Wall
landmarks.nasaQuery: cosmic web dark matter galaxy filament
funFacts: A colossal cosmic filament wall of galaxies stretching 1.37 billion light-years across—roughly 1/60th the diameter of the entire Observable Universe!

landmarks.name: TON 618 Ultramassive Quasar
landmarks.nasaQuery: quasar supermassive black hole jet artist
funFacts: Powered by one of the largest black holes ever measured (~40–66 billion solar masses)—an event horizon 1,300 AU across (32× Neptune’s orbit!).
Its accretion disk shines as brightly as 140 TRILLION Suns, outshining our entire Milky Way galaxy 2,000 times over.

landmarks.name: JADES-GS-z14-0 (JWST Earliest Galaxy)
funFacts: Spectroscopically confirmed at redshift z = 14.32—we see its light from just 290 million years after the Big Bang!
Because cosmic expansion stretched space while its photons traveled for 13.5 billion years, this galaxy currently sits ~33.8 billion light-years from Earth.

landmarks.name: Cosmic Microwave Background (Observable Horizon)
funFacts: Marks the spherical boundary of the Observable Universe (~46.5 billion light-years radius, 93 billion light-years diameter in comoving coordinates).
Relic thermal afterglow emitted 380,000 years after the Big Bang when the 3,000 K primordial plasma cooled into neutral hydrogen—now redshifted to 2.725 K.
Our Solar System’s motion creates a measurable Doppler dipole across the CMB, proving we are hurtling at 369.82 km/s toward Leo!
